title: Shared Figures, Different Tellings
bigQuestion: When the Qur'an and the Bible tell a story about the same person, what changes, what stays, and why does each telling make sense to its readers?

story.title: The Son on the Mountain
story.kicker: One father, one knife, one ram in the thicket. Three scriptures tell it, and the son does not always have the same name.
paragraphs: Ms. Okafor put three books on the table at the front of the room. A King James Bible from 1611, in a modern printing. A Jewish Publication Society Bible from 1917. And Marmaduke Pickthall's 1930 English rendering of the Qur'an. 'Same story,' she said. 'Three tellings. Find the differences.' She wrote on the board: Genesis 22 and Surah 37, verses 99 to 113.

Priya read the Genesis version first. God tells Abraham to take his son Isaac to the land of Moriah and offer him up. Abraham goes. Isaac carries the wood and asks where the lamb is. Abraham binds him on the altar. An angel stops the knife. A ram is caught in a thicket. The JPS 1917 text said the same thing in slightly different words, because it was translated from the same Hebrew.

Then Marcus read Pickthall. Ibrahim (Abraham) tells his son he has seen in a dream that he must sacrifice him, and asks what the boy thinks. The son answers that his father should do what he is commanded. Both submit. God calls out that the vision has been fulfilled, and ransoms the son with a great sacrifice. Marcus stopped. 'It doesn't say which son.' He read it again. It did not. A few verses later the text announces good news of Ishaq (Isaac), a prophet to come.

'So who was on the mountain?' Ms. Okafor asked. Priya said Isaac, because Genesis names him. Marcus said the Qur'an leaves it open, and then mentions Isaac as if he came after. Ms. Okafor nodded. 'Muslim commentators argued about exactly this for centuries. Al-Tabari, writing around the year 900, recorded both views. Most later Muslim scholars settled on Ismail (Ishmael). Many Jewish and Christian readers never had the question, because their text names Isaac in the first line.'

She held up all three books. 'This unit is about reading side by side. Not to pick the winner. To see what each book assumes, what it stresses, and what its readers have done with it. Notice the Qur'an never tells you the son's name, the place, or the ram. It expects you to know the story already. That is a clue about who was listening.'
story.think: The Qur'an's telling leaves out the son's name and the mountain. Why might a text skip details that its first hearers already knew, and what does that do to a reader who does not know them?

lessons.title: What the Qur'an Assumes You Know
lessons.mainIdea: The Qur'an retells stories from the Bible in short, pointed form, often assuming its first hearers already knew the outline.
reading: The Qur'an names about twenty-five prophets, and most of them also appear in the Hebrew Bible or the New Testament. Adam, Nuh (Noah), Ibrahim (Abraham), Yusuf (Joseph), Musa (Moses), Dawud (David), Sulayman (Solomon), Yunus (Jonah), Maryam (Mary) and Isa (Jesus) all have a place in it. But the Qur'an does not tell their stories the way Genesis or the Gospels do. It usually gives a scene, a speech, or a lesson, then moves on. Scholars call this style *allusive*: it points to a story rather than narrating it from start to finish.

Take Nuh (Noah). Surah 71 is named for him, and Surah 11 tells the flood in some detail. But nowhere does the Qur'an give the ark's measurements, the forty days of rain, or the dove with the olive leaf. Instead it stresses Noah's long preaching, his people's refusal, and one son who would not board. Genesis 6 to 9 has none of that son and all of the measurements. Each book tells the part that serves its purpose.

Historians of the Qur'an note that Mecca and Medina in the 600s had Jewish and Christian neighbors, and Arabic-speaking traders knew biblical stories from hearing them told. Muslims believe the Qur'an confirms earlier scripture (a claim it makes in 2:97 and 3:3). Whichever way a reader explains it, the text often works like a reminder. The Qur'an even uses that word for itself: *dhikr*, a reminder. Reading side by side lets you see what it reminds its hearers of and what it changes.

This lesson gives you a method. First, find the passage in each book. Second, list what each one includes and leaves out. Third, ask what each telling stresses. Fourth, and only then, ask how readers in each tradition have explained the differences. Jews, Christians and Muslims have all done this work for over a thousand years. Your job is to describe their readings fairly, not to rule on them.

words.d: pointing to a story or idea without telling it in full
Arabic for 'reminder' or 'remembrance'; one of the Qur'an's names for itself
in the Qur'an, a person Muslims believe God chose to carry a message to a people
placing two texts next to each other to compare what each includes, leaves out and stresses

look.title: Two Floods
look.text: Genesis 6 to 9 gives the ark's size in cubits, the animals two by two, forty days of rain, a raven and a dove, and a rainbow as a sign of promise. Surah 11:25 to 49 gives Noah's long argument with his people, their mockery while he builds, the command to load the ark, a son who refuses to board and drowns, and the ark coming to rest on Mount Judi. Neither book contradicts the other's outline, but each keeps different details.
look.prompt: Pick one detail that only Genesis keeps and one that only the Qur'an keeps. What does each choice tell you about what that book wants its reader to take away?

check.q: What does it mean to say the Qur'an's storytelling is allusive?
choices: It tells each story from beginning to end
It points to a story its hearers know rather than narrating it in full
It only tells stories that are not in the Bible
It uses no names for the prophets
check.why: Allusive means pointing to a story rather than narrating every detail; the Qur'an assumes the outline is known.

check.q: Which detail appears in the Qur'an's flood story but not in Genesis?
choices: A son of Noah who refuses to board
A dove with an olive leaf
check.why: Surah 11 tells of Noah's son who would not board; Genesis gives the measurements, the dove and the rainbow instead.

check.q: What is the recommended last step of side-by-side reading?
choices: Count how many verses each passage has
Find the passage in each book
Ask how readers in each tradition have explained the differences
check.why: The method ends by describing how each tradition's readers have handled the differences, not by ruling on them.

lessons.title: Three Texts and Their Translations
lessons.mainIdea: To compare fairly, use translations you can cite: KJV (1611) and JPS (1917) for the Bible, Pickthall (1930) for the Qur'an.
reading: A comparison is only as good as the texts on the table. The Hebrew Bible, which Jews call the *Tanakh*, was written in Hebrew with a little Aramaic. The New Testament was written in Greek. The Qur'an was recited in Arabic, and Muslims hold that only the Arabic is the Qur'an itself; an English version is a rendering of its meaning. So when this course reads side by side, it is reading three translations, and it names each one.

For the Bible we use two public-domain translations. The King James Version of 1611 was made by English scholars for the Church of England and shaped English for centuries. The Jewish Publication Society translation of 1917 was made by American Jewish scholars in Philadelphia and follows the Hebrew order of the books. Both are old, so their English can sound formal, with 'thee' and 'thou' and 'saith'. For the Qur'an we use Marmaduke Pickthall's The Meaning of the Glorious Koran (1930). Pickthall was an English convert to Islam, and his title itself says the book is a rendering of meaning.

Translators make choices. Pickthall keeps 'Allah' rather than 'God'. He writes the prophets' names in their Arabic forms, so you will see Ibrahim, Musa and Isa, while the KJV and JPS write Abraham, Moses and Jesus. Pickthall's English is deliberately old-fashioned, close to the KJV's sound. This can make the two books feel alike on the page even when their content differs, so read for meaning, not for tone.

One more rule: modern translations like Yusuf Ali (1934) or Arberry (1955) are still under copyright, so this course describes them but does not quote them. When you cite a passage, give the book, chapter and verse or surah and ayah, the translator and the year. That is what lets another reader check your work.

words.d: the Jewish name for the Hebrew Bible: Torah, Prophets and Writings
the English Bible of 1611 made for the Church of England; public domain
the Jewish Publication Society's English Tanakh, published in Philadelphia in 1917
Marmaduke Pickthall, English convert to Islam whose 1930 Qur'an translation this course reads

look.title: The Texts on the Table
rows: Qur'an revealed, per Muslim tradition, from
look.cite: Dates are the rounded figures used in standard introductions to each scripture; scholars debate the earlier ones
look.prompt: About how many centuries separate the Gospels from the Qur'an, and the Qur'an from the first English translation we quote? Why does that gap matter for comparison?

check.q: Which translation follows the Hebrew order of the books of the Bible?
check.why: The Jewish Publication Society's 1917 Tanakh follows the Hebrew order; the KJV follows the Christian order.

check.q: Why does Pickthall's title say 'The Meaning of the Glorious Koran'?
choices: Muslims hold that only the Arabic is the Qur'an, so an English version renders its meaning
He translated only part of the book
It was the name of his mosque
He wanted to sound like the King James Bible
check.why: Muslims hold the Arabic alone is the Qur'an; a translation gives the meaning, and Pickthall's title says so.

check.q: Which of these should you include when you cite a passage in this course?
choices: Book, chapter and verse or surah and ayah, translator and year
check.why: A full citation names the text, the reference, the translator and the year so a reader can check it.

lessons.title: Adam: One Garden, Two Emphases
lessons.mainIdea: Genesis and the Qur'an both tell of Adam's creation and the garden, but the Qur'an stresses the angels' bow, Iblis's refusal and Adam's forgiveness.
reading: Genesis 2 and 3 tell how God forms the man from dust, plants a garden in Eden, makes the woman from his side, and forbids one tree. A serpent persuades the woman, she eats, the man eats, and both are sent out of the garden. Genesis names the woman Eve and lists the consequences: pain, hard work, and the ground cursed. Christians later read this story as the origin of sin for all people; Jewish readers generally did not read it that way.

The Qur'an tells Adam's story in several places, most fully in 2:30 to 39, 7:11 to 25 and 20:115 to 123. Here are the parts it stresses. God announces to the angels that he will place a *khalifa*, a deputy or successor, on the earth. God teaches Adam the names of all things, and the angels cannot match him. God commands the angels to bow to Adam. All do except *Iblis*, who refuses out of pride. Adam and his wife (she is not named in the Qur'an) are warned against one tree, are tempted by Satan together, both eat, and both are sent down.

Then comes the difference readers notice most. In 2:37 the Qur'an says Adam received words from his Lord and God relented toward him. Muslims read this as Adam being forgiven on the spot. Mainstream Muslim teaching therefore holds that no guilt passes to Adam's children; each person is born without sin and answers for their own deeds. Pickthall's rendering of 2:37 says the Lord 'relented toward him,' and Muslim commentators such as Ibn Kathir (d. 1373) point to it as the moment of pardon.

Reading side by side, you can see three scriptures and three emphases. Genesis narrates the loss of the garden and its costs. Christian readers, following Paul in Romans 5, often read Adam as the one through whom sin entered the world. The Qur'an narrates the honor of Adam, the fall of Iblis, and a quick forgiveness. None of these readings is a mistake about the others; each is a reading of its own book.

words.d: Arabic for deputy or successor; the Qur'an's word for Adam's role on earth
the being who refused to bow to Adam in the Qur'an; also called Shaytan (Satan)
the Christian teaching that Adam's disobedience passed guilt or a fallen state to all people
the garden in Genesis 2 where the first humans lived

look.title: Who Ate First?
look.text: Genesis 3:6 (KJV) has the woman take the fruit and eat, then give some to her husband, who eats. Qur'an 7:20 to 22 (Pickthall's rendering, paraphrased) has Satan whisper to both of them together, and both taste the tree together, after which both see their shame and God calls to both. Later Christian writers sometimes blamed Eve; the Qur'an's telling gives no order and no separate blame.
look.prompt: How might a text that says 'both together' lead its readers to think differently about women than a text that says 'she first, then he'? Which readers in each tradition might resist the simple version?

check.q: What does the Qur'an say happened right after Adam's disobedience, according to 2:37?
choices: Adam was cursed for all time
God relented toward Adam, which Muslims read as forgiveness
check.why: Qur'an 2:37 says Adam received words from his Lord and God relented toward him; Muslims read this as pardon.

check.q: Who refused to bow to Adam in the Qur'an's account?
check.why: In 2:34 and 7:11 all the angels bow except Iblis, who refuses out of pride.

check.q: Which of these is a difference between Genesis 3 and the Qur'an's telling?
choices: Genesis has the woman eat first; the Qur'an has both eat together
The Qur'an names the woman Eve; Genesis does not
The Qur'an sets the story in Egypt
check.why: Genesis 3:6 has the woman eat first, then the man; Qur'an 7:20 to 22 describes both together. The Qur'an does not name her.

lessons.title: Ibrahim: Friend of God, Builder of the Kaaba
lessons.mainIdea: Both books make Abraham the father of faith, but the Qur'an adds a Meccan chapter: Ibrahim and Ismail raising the Kaaba.
reading: Abraham is the figure the three traditions share most fully, and the one they claim most strongly. Genesis 12 to 25 tells his call, his journey to Canaan, the covenant, the birth of Ishmael to Hagar and of Isaac to Sarah, and the sending away of Hagar and Ishmael into the wilderness. The Qur'an calls him Ibrahim and names him a *hanif*, one who turned from idols to the one God, and *khalil Allah*, the friend of God (4:125). Surah 14 is named for him.

The Qur'an tells scenes Genesis does not. In 6:74 to 79 and 21:51 to 70, young Ibrahim argues with his father and his people about their idols, smashes the idols, and is thrown into a fire that God makes cool for him. Jewish readers will recognize the fire: a rabbinic midrash in Genesis Rabbah tells a similar story of Abraham and the furnace of Nimrod. Historians note this as one of many places where the Qur'an and Jewish tradition seem to share a pool of stories beyond the Bible's text.

The biggest addition is Mecca. In 2:125 to 129, Ibrahim and his son Ismail (Ishmael) raise the foundations of the House, the *Kaaba*, and pray that God will send their descendants a messenger. Muslims read that messenger as Muhammad. Nothing in Genesis brings Abraham to Arabia; Genesis 21 leaves Hagar and Ishmael in the wilderness of Paran. Muslim tradition says Ibrahim brought them to the valley of Mecca, and the pilgrimage rites (running between the hills of Safa and Marwa, the well of Zamzam) retell Hagar's search for water.

So each tradition draws its own line from Abraham. Jews trace the covenant through Isaac and Jacob (Israel). Christians, following Paul in Galatians 3, read Abraham's faith as the model for faith in Christ. Muslims read Ibrahim as the first Muslim in the plain sense of the word, one who submitted, and as the ancestor of the Arabs through Ismail. Qur'an 3:67 says Ibrahim was neither Jew nor Christian but a hanif who submitted. Each claim is a reading of a shared ancestor.

words.d: in the Qur'an, a person who turned from idols to worship the one God before Islam
the cube-shaped House in Mecca that Muslims believe Ibrahim and Ismail built or rebuilt
Jewish interpretive storytelling that fills gaps in the Bible's text
a binding agreement; in Genesis, God's promise to Abraham and his descendants

look.title: Raising the House
look.text: In Pickthall's rendering of 2:127, Abraham and Ishmael raise the foundations of the House and pray that their Lord accept the work from them, for he is the Hearer, the Knower. In the verses that follow they ask God to make them submissive, to show them their rites, and to raise up among their descendants a messenger who will recite God's revelations and teach the Scripture.
look.cite: Qur'an 2:127 to 129, Surah Al-Baqarah, Marmaduke Pickthall, The Meaning of the Glorious Koran, 1930
look.prompt: Muslims read the 'messenger' in this prayer as Muhammad. What does the prayer do for a Meccan hearer who already treasured the Kaaba?

check.q: What does the Qur'an say Ibrahim and Ismail did in Mecca, in 2:127?
choices: Raised the foundations of the House, the Kaaba
check.why: Qur'an 2:127 says Ibrahim and Ismail raised the foundations of the House; Muslim tradition identifies it as the Kaaba.

check.q: Which story appears in the Qur'an and in Jewish midrash but not in the text of Genesis?
choices: Abraham thrown into a fire and saved
check.why: The furnace story is in Qur'an 21 and in Genesis Rabbah, but Genesis itself does not tell it.

check.q: How does Qur'an 3:67 describe Ibrahim?
choices: As a hanif who submitted, neither Jew nor Christian
check.why: Qur'an 3:67 says Abraham was neither Jew nor Christian but a hanif who submitted to God.

lessons.title: Ismail and Isaac: The Unnamed Son
lessons.mainIdea: Genesis names Isaac as the son Abraham was told to sacrifice; the Qur'an leaves the son unnamed, and Muslim scholars came to read him as Ismail.
reading: Genesis 22 is one of the most studied chapters in the Bible. God tests Abraham, telling him to take his son Isaac to Moriah and offer him up. Jewish tradition calls the story the *Akedah*, the Binding, and reads it in synagogue on the New Year. Christians have often read Isaac carrying the wood as a picture of Jesus carrying the cross. In the KJV the command names the son at once: 'Take now thy son, thine only son Isaac, whom thou lovest.'

The Qur'an's version in 37:99 to 113 never names the son. Ibrahim prays for a righteous child and is given good news of a gentle boy. When the boy is old enough to walk with him, Ibrahim tells him of a dream in which he sacrifices him and asks what he thinks. The boy tells his father to do as he is commanded. Both submit, Ibrahim lays him down, and God calls out that the vision is fulfilled and ransoms him with a great sacrifice. Then, in 37:112, the text gives good news of Ishaq (Isaac), a prophet.

That last verse is why Muslim commentators argued. If Isaac is announced after the sacrifice, some reasoned, the boy on the mountain must be the other son, Ismail. Others held that the boy was Isaac, as the Bible says, and al-Tabari (d. 923) reports both views with their supporting reports. Over the following centuries the view that the son was Ismail became the mainstream Muslim position, tied to the Kaaba story and to the festival of *Eid al-Adha*, which commemorates the sacrifice.

Two features of the Qur'an's telling stand out beside Genesis. First, the son is asked and consents; in Genesis he asks where the lamb is and is not told. Second, the Qur'an gives no place, no wood, no altar and no ram, only 'a great sacrifice.' Read one way, this is a text that assumes its hearers know the scene. Read another way, it is a text that shifts the focus from the father's obedience alone to the shared submission of father and son. Both readings are found among Muslim commentators.

words.d: Hebrew for 'binding'; the Jewish name for the story of Abraham and Isaac in Genesis 22
the Muslim festival of sacrifice, tied to Ibrahim's willingness to offer his son
Muslim historian and commentator (d. 923) whose tafsir records earlier scholars' views
a scholar who writes explanations of a scripture, verse by verse

look.title: The Command in Genesis
look.text: And he said, Take now thy son, thine only son Isaac, whom thou lovest, and get thee into the land of Moriah; and offer him there for a burnt offering upon one of the mountains which I will tell thee of.
look.prompt: This verse names the son, the place and the act in one sentence. Compare it with Qur'an 37:102, where the father tells the son about a dream and asks his view. What does each opening ask its reader to feel?

check.q: Which son does Qur'an 37:102 name as the one to be sacrificed?
check.why: The Qur'an's telling in Surah 37 leaves the son unnamed; commentators supplied the name later.

check.q: What did al-Tabari do with the question of which son it was?
choices: He ruled that it was Jacob
He said the Qur'an forbids asking
He recorded both the Isaac view and the Ismail view
check.why: Al-Tabari's tafsir reports both views with their supporting traditions, a typical feature of his method.

check.q: What is the Jewish name for the story in Genesis 22?
check.why: Akedah means binding; the story is read in synagogue at Rosh Hashanah, the New Year.

lessons.title: Yusuf: The Best of Stories
lessons.mainIdea: Joseph is the one biblical figure whose story the Qur'an tells in full, in a single surah, and comparing it with Genesis shows how the Qur'an shapes a story.
reading: The Qur'an calls Surah 12 'the best of stories' (12:3) and tells the story of Yusuf (Joseph) from beginning to end in 111 verses. This is unusual; almost every other biblical figure appears in pieces across many surahs. Genesis 37 to 50 tells the same story: a favored son, jealous brothers, a pit, slavery in Egypt, a master's wife, prison, dreams interpreted, rise to power, famine, and the brothers' return. The two versions run in parallel more closely than any other pair in this unit.

The differences are in what each version keeps. Genesis gives names: Potiphar, Reuben, Judah, Benjamin, Pharaoh. The Qur'an names only Yusuf and his father Yaqub (Jacob); the master is 'the Aziz,' the wife is unnamed, and the brothers are unnamed. Genesis gives the coat of many colors; the Qur'an gives a shirt, first stained with false blood, then torn from behind (12:26 to 28), then sent home to restore Yaqub's sight (12:93). The shirt works as a thread through the whole surah.

Some scenes are only in the Qur'an. The master's wife invites the women of the city to a meal, gives them knives, and has Yusuf walk in; they cut their hands in astonishment (12:31). Yusuf preaches to his fellow prisoners about the one God before he interprets their dreams (12:37 to 40). At the end Yusuf prays to be taken as a Muslim, one who submits (12:101). Genesis has none of these; it has Joseph weep in private and, at the very end, forgive his brothers and speak of God's purpose (Genesis 50:20).

Muslim commentators read Surah 12 as a story about patience, God's plan, and the lure of a beautiful person, and Sufi poets like Jami (d. 1492) turned Yusuf and the wife, whom later tradition names Zulaykha, into a poem about longing for God. Jewish readers have long treated Joseph as the one who preserved his brothers and kept faith in exile. Christian readers sometimes saw in the rejected brother who saves his family a foreshadowing of Jesus. One story, told twice, has fed three sets of readers.

words.d: the Arabic name of Joseph, son of Jacob; Surah 12 is named for him
the title the Qur'an gives Joseph's Egyptian master, 'the mighty one'
the name later Muslim tradition gives the master's wife; the Qur'an leaves her unnamed
reading an earlier story as a hint of a later one

look.title: The Torn Shirt
look.text: In Qur'an 12:26 to 28, a witness from the wife's household says: if Yusuf's shirt is torn from the front, she is telling the truth; if it is torn from behind, he is. The shirt is torn from behind, and the master says the wife has schemed. Genesis 39 has the wife keep Joseph's garment as false evidence and has Potiphar throw Joseph into prison without any test. Both versions have Joseph end up in prison, but by different routes.
look.prompt: The Qur'an's version proves Yusuf innocent yet still sends him to prison (12:35). What does each book seem to want its reader to notice about justice and about Joseph's character?

check.q: How is the story of Yusuf different from most other biblical figures in the Qur'an?
choices: It appears only in Meccan hadith
It is told in full in one surah rather than in pieces
It contradicts Genesis at every point
check.why: Surah 12 tells Joseph's story from start to finish in one place, unlike the scattered mentions of most prophets.

check.q: Which scene is in the Qur'an's Joseph story but not in Genesis?
choices: Joseph rises to power in Egypt
The women of the city cut their hands at the sight of Yusuf
check.why: The banquet where the women cut their hands (12:31) has no parallel in Genesis 37 to 50.

check.q: Who is Zulaykha?
choices: A name later Muslim tradition gives the master's wife
check.why: The Qur'an does not name the wife; later Muslim tradition and Persian poetry call her Zulaykha.

sections.title: Musa, Kings and a Prophet in the Fish

lessons.title: Musa: The Most Mentioned Prophet
lessons.mainIdea: Moses appears more often than anyone else in the Qur'an, with the burning bush, Pharaoh, the sea and Sinai, told as scenes and speeches rather than one long narrative.
reading: By most counts Musa (Moses) is named about 136 times in the Qur'an, more than any other person. His story is spread across many surahs, with Surah 20 (Ta Ha), Surah 28 (Al-Qasas, The Story) and Surah 26 (Ash-Shu'ara) giving the longest stretches. Exodus, Numbers and Deuteronomy tell the same life in the Hebrew Bible. Muslim readers have often noted that Muhammad's own career, as tradition tells it, echoed Musa's: a prophet sent to a stubborn people, then a migration.

The shared scenes are easy to find. God speaks to Musa from a fire at the sacred valley of Tuwa (20:9 to 24; Exodus 3). Musa's staff becomes a serpent and his hand shines white (20:17 to 22; Exodus 4). He confronts Pharaoh (Firawn) and the magicians, who in the Qur'an fall down as believers (20:70; Exodus 7 to 8 has no conversion). The sea is parted (26:63; Exodus 14). Israel receives tablets at the mountain and makes a golden calf (20:83 to 98; Exodus 32).

The differences are small but telling. In the Qur'an the calf is made not by Aaron (Harun) but by a figure called al-Samiri (20:85 to 97), and Harun is cleared of blame. In Exodus 32 Aaron makes the calf himself. The Qur'an also tells a story with no biblical parallel: Musa travels with a mysterious servant of God, unnamed in the text but called al-Khidr in tradition, who does three shocking things and then explains them (18:60 to 82). Muslim commentators read it as a lesson about the limits of human knowledge.

Both books call Moses a lawgiver. The Qur'an says the Torah (Tawrat) was given to him with guidance and light (5:44). It calls the Israelites the Children of Israel (Bani Israil) and Surah 17 opens with that name. Jewish readers see in Exodus the founding of a people bound by covenant; Muslim readers see in Musa's story the pattern of every prophet and a warning about a people who received a book and, in the Qur'an's view, sometimes strayed from it. Neither reading is the whole of either book.

words.d: the Qur'an's name for Pharaoh, the king who opposed Musa
the Arabic name for the Torah, the book the Qur'an says was given to Musa
the figure who, in Qur'an 20, makes the golden calf; Aaron is cleared
the name tradition gives the wise servant of God who travels with Musa in Surah 18

look.title: How Often Each Prophet Is Named
look.cite: Standard concordance counts of proper names in the Arabic text; scholars' totals differ by a few because of spelling forms
look.prompt: Moses is named about five times as often as Jesus. What might that tell you about the audience the Qur'an addressed and the model of prophethood it stresses?

check.q: Who makes the golden calf in the Qur'an's telling?
check.why: Qur'an 20:85 to 97 blames al-Samiri and clears Harun; Exodus 32 has Aaron make the calf.

check.q: Which story about Musa has no parallel in the Bible?
choices: The journey with a wise servant of God (Surah 18)
check.why: The journey with the unnamed servant, called al-Khidr in tradition, is found only in Qur'an 18:60 to 82.

check.q: What does Qur'an 5:44 say about the Torah?
choices: That it is the same as the Qur'an
That it was revealed with guidance and light
check.why: Qur'an 5:44 says God revealed the Torah with guidance and light; Muslims read this as honoring the earlier book.

lessons.title: Dawud and Sulayman: Psalms, Ants and a Queen
lessons.mainIdea: In the Qur'an David and Solomon are prophets and kings who receive a book and command birds and jinn, while the Bible remembers their reigns, their psalms and their faults.
reading: The Hebrew Bible tells David's life at length in 1 and 2 Samuel: shepherd, giant-killer, outlaw, king, and sinner who takes Bathsheba and is rebuked by the prophet Nathan. Tradition links him to the Psalms. His son Solomon builds the Temple in Jerusalem, judges wisely, receives the Queen of Sheba, and in 1 Kings 11 turns to other gods in old age. The Bible presents both as great kings with real failings.

The Qur'an knows Dawud (David) as a prophet-king who killed Jalut (Goliath) (2:251) and received a book called the *Zabur*, usually identified with the Psalms (4:163, 17:55). Mountains and birds praise God with him (21:79, 34:10). It also tells a scene of two disputants who climb into his prayer chamber; Dawud judges hastily, then asks forgiveness and is forgiven (38:21 to 25). Most Muslim commentators read this as a lesson in judgment; a few early ones linked it to the Bathsheba story, but the mainstream rejected that, since Muslims hold prophets are protected from grave sin.

Sulayman (Solomon) gets even more color. The wind is subjected to him and the *jinn* work for him (34:12). He understands the speech of birds and hears an ant warn its fellows to get out of his army's path (27:16 to 19). A hoopoe brings news of a queen in Sheba who worships the sun; Sulayman writes to her, a jinn brings her throne, and she enters a palace floor of glass she mistakes for water and submits to God (27:20 to 44). The Bible's Queen of Sheba (1 Kings 10) comes to test Solomon with riddles and goes home impressed, with no conversion.

Reading side by side, the pattern of the chapter repeats. The Bible keeps the politics and the failures; the Qur'an keeps the prophethood and the signs, and where the Bible reports a sin it either leaves it out or turns it toward repentance. Jewish and Christian readers do not think less of their text for its candor; they read the failings as part of its honesty. Muslim readers do not see a gap in theirs; they read it as a book about what prophets are for. Each set of readers has its own reasons.

look.prompt: The two visits end differently: one with praise and gifts, one with submission to God. What does each ending suggest about what the story is for in that book?

lessons.title: Yunus: The Prophet Who Ran
lessons.mainIdea: Jonah's story is nearly the same in both books, but the Qur'an stresses his prayer inside the fish and his people's repentance rather than his anger at Nineveh.
reading: The Book of Jonah is four short chapters in the Hebrew Bible. God sends Jonah to Nineveh; he flees by ship; a storm rises; the sailors throw him overboard; a great fish swallows him; he prays; the fish spits him out; he preaches; Nineveh repents; and Jonah sulks under a withered plant while God asks whether he should not pity a great city. Jews read it in synagogue on the afternoon of Yom Kippur, the Day of Atonement, because it is a story about repentance accepted.

The Qur'an names Yunus (Jonah) in Surah 10, which bears his name, and tells the story mainly in 37:139 to 148 and 21:87 to 88. Yunus goes to the ship, draws lots, is swallowed by the fish, and calls out from the darkness. He is cast onto the shore, a gourd plant grows over him, and he is sent to a city of a hundred thousand or more, who believe. In 68:48 to 50 he is called 'the companion of the fish' and the reader is told not to be like him in his haste. The Qur'an never names Nineveh and never tells the ending under the plant.

The heart of the Qur'an's version is the prayer. In 21:87 Yunus calls out from the darkness that there is no god but God, that God is glorified, and that he himself has been among the wrongdoers. Muslims often recite this line in distress; hadith collections record the Prophet recommending it. In the Bible, Jonah's prayer in chapter 2 is a full psalm of thanksgiving from the belly of the fish. The two prayers have the same setting and different moods: one confesses wrong, one gives thanks.

Notice what the Qur'an keeps and drops. It keeps the disobedience, the fish, the plant, and the city that believed. It drops the argument between Jonah and God over pity for Nineveh, which is the Bible's whole last chapter. Jewish and Christian readers have read that argument as the point of the book. Muslim commentators read Yunus's story as a warning about impatience in a prophet and a proof that a whole people can turn and be spared. Same fish, different lesson.

words.d: the Arabic name of Jonah; Surah 10 is named for him
the Assyrian city Jonah is sent to in the Bible; unnamed in the Qur'an
the Jewish Day of Atonement, when the Book of Jonah is read
turning away from wrongdoing and back toward God; a theme in both tellings

look.title: A Cry from the Dark
look.text: In Pickthall's rendering of 21:87, Dhun-Nun (the one of the fish) goes off in anger, thinking God has no power over him, and then cries out in the darkness that there is no God save Thee, be Thou glorified, and that he has been a wrong-doer. In 21:88 God answers him and saves him from the anguish, and the verse adds that this is how God saves believers.
look.cite: Qur'an 21:87 to 88, Surah Al-Anbiya, Marmaduke Pickthall, The Meaning of the Glorious Koran, 1930
look.prompt: Compare this cry with Jonah 2 in the KJV, a long psalm of thanks. What does each prayer say about the relationship between the prophet and God at that moment?

check.why: The Qur'an keeps the fish, the plant and the believing city but has no scene of Jonah disputing God's mercy.

check.q: When do Jews read the Book of Jonah in synagogue?
check.why: Jonah is read on the afternoon of Yom Kippur, the Day of Atonement, because it is about repentance accepted.

check.q: What does Yunus say in his prayer in Qur'an 21:87?

lessons.title: Maryam: The Only Woman Named
lessons.mainIdea: Mary is the only woman the Qur'an names, and Surah 19 tells her story with a birth scene and a speaking infant that the Gospels do not have.
reading: The Qur'an names Maryam (Mary) about 34 times, more often than the New Testament does, and she is the only woman it names at all. Surah 19 is named for her, and Surah 3 tells of her mother's vow, her childhood in the sanctuary under the care of Zakariya (Zechariah), and the food she was given from God (3:35 to 37). The Gospels of Matthew and Luke tell of Mary's betrothal to Joseph, the angel's announcement, the journey to Bethlehem and the birth in a manger. The Qur'an mentions none of those settings and never names Joseph.

Both books have an annunciation. In Luke 1:26 to 38 the angel Gabriel tells Mary she will bear a son, and she asks how, since she has known no man. In Qur'an 19:16 to 21 a spirit sent from God appears to Maryam in the form of a man; she asks the same question, and is told it is easy for God. Christians and Muslims agree that Mary conceived Jesus without a father, though they read what that means very differently, as the next lesson shows.

The birth scene is the Qur'an's own. Maryam withdraws to a distant place, is seized by labor pains at the trunk of a palm tree, and cries out that she wishes she had died. A voice tells her not to grieve: a stream runs below her, and if she shakes the palm, ripe dates will fall (19:22 to 26). She brings the child to her people, who accuse her; she points to the baby, and Isa (Jesus) speaks from the cradle, declaring himself a servant of God given a scripture and made a prophet (19:27 to 33). The canonical Gospels have no palm, no stream and no speaking infant.

Historians note that a speaking infant Jesus and a palm tree that feeds Mary appear in Christian texts outside the New Testament, such as the Arabic Infancy Gospel and the Gospel of Pseudo-Matthew, which circulated in the centuries before Islam. Muslim commentators such as al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir treat the Qur'an's account as the true report and read the palm scene as a sign of God's care. Christian readers, whose Bible does not include those texts, mostly encounter the scene as new. Both sets of readers see in it a Mary honored for her purity and trust.

words.d: the Arabic name of Mary, mother of Jesus; the only woman named in the Qur'an
the announcement to Mary that she will bear a son, told in Luke 1 and Qur'an 19
Zechariah, the priest who cared for Maryam in the sanctuary and was father of Yahya (John)
an early Christian text about Jesus's childhood that is not in the New Testament

look.title: Two Annunciations
look.text: Luke 1:30 to 35 (KJV): the angel Gabriel greets Mary, tells her not to fear, that she will conceive and bear a son named Jesus who will be called the Son of the Highest and reign over the house of Jacob forever; Mary asks how this can be; the angel says the Holy Ghost will come upon her. Qur'an 19:17 to 21 (Pickthall, paraphrased): a spirit sent from God appears to Maryam as a man; she asks for protection; he says he is a messenger sent to give her a pure boy; she asks how, having known no man; he says it is easy for God, a sign for mankind and a mercy.

lessons.title: Isa: Prophet and Messiah, Not Divine
lessons.mainIdea: The Qur'an honors Jesus as a prophet, a word from God and the Messiah, while denying that he is God or God's son, which is the central difference between Islam and Christianity.
reading: The Qur'an calls Isa (Jesus) 'the Messiah' (al-Masih) eleven times, 'a word from God' (3:45), 'a spirit from Him' (4:171), and a messenger who was given the *Injil*, the Gospel (5:46). It tells of his virgin birth, his miracles by God's leave, including healing the blind and the leper and raising the dead (3:49; 5:110), and his disciples. No other prophet in the Qur'an is given such titles. Muslims regard Isa as one of the greatest messengers and believe he will return before the end of time, though that return is drawn mainly from hadith rather than from the Qur'an's own text.

At the same time the Qur'an denies what Christians affirm most. Surah 112, which many Muslims recite daily, says God 'begetteth not nor was begotten.' Qur'an 5:72 says those who say God is the Messiah have disbelieved, and 5:73 rejects the claim that God is 'the third of three.' Qur'an 4:171 tells the People of the Book not to say 'Three' and calls Isa a messenger and a word, not a son. Muslim scholars read these verses as protecting *tawhid*, the oneness of God. Christian scholars read the New Testament, especially John 1, as teaching that the Word who was with God became flesh in Jesus.

It helps to state both positions precisely. Mainstream Christianity, as defined at the councils of Nicaea (325) and Chalcedon (451), holds that Jesus is fully God and fully human, one person of the Trinity. The Qur'an, as Muslims read it, holds that Jesus is a created human being, a prophet, born of a virgin by God's command, who never claimed divinity (5:116 has Isa deny telling people to worship him and his mother). Some historians suggest the Qur'an's 'third of three' may address a local form of Christian belief; Muslim commentators generally read it as addressing the Trinity itself.

The disagreement is real and old, and this course does not settle it. What it can do is show how each side reads. Christians point to the Gospels and letters written within decades of Jesus's life. Muslims point to the Qur'an, which they believe corrects what earlier communities altered, a claim the next chapter examines. Both traditions honor Mary and Jesus; both reject the other's central claim about him. Describing that fairly, in each tradition's own words, is what a careful comparison looks like.

words.d: the Messiah; the title the Qur'an gives Isa eleven times
the Arabic name for the Gospel, the book the Qur'an says was given to Isa
the Muslim doctrine that God is one, without partner, parent or child
the Christian doctrine that the one God is Father, Son and Holy Spirit
the church council of 325 that defined Jesus as fully divine, of one being with the Father

lessons.title: The Cross: 4:157 and Its Readers
lessons.mainIdea: Most Muslims read Qur'an 4:157 to mean Jesus was not crucified but was raised to God, while Christians hold the crucifixion as history and as the center of faith.
reading: All four Gospels end Jesus's life with his crucifixion under the Roman governor Pontius Pilate and his burial, followed by the resurrection. Historians of the ancient world, whatever their faith, generally accept the crucifixion as one of the best attested facts about Jesus, since it is reported by Christian, Jewish and Roman sources. For Christians it is the center of their faith: Paul writes in 1 Corinthians 15 that Christ died for sins and was raised.

The Qur'an addresses the cross once, in 4:157, in a passage listing charges against certain Israelites. Pickthall renders the key clause: 'they slew him not nor crucified him, but it appeared so unto them.' The next verse says God raised him to himself (4:158). From early on, most Muslim commentators read this to mean Jesus was not killed at all. Many, following reports in al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir, held that another person was made to look like Jesus and was crucified in his place, while Jesus was taken up alive. This is the substitution reading.

Not every Muslim reader agreed on the details. Some classical commentators recorded several candidates for the substitute and admitted uncertainty. A few readers, ancient and modern, have argued that the verse denies only that Jesus's enemies succeeded in defeating him, not that he died; others, like the Ahmadiyya movement, hold that he survived the cross. Mainstream Sunni and Shia scholars maintain the view that Jesus was not crucified and was raised alive, and that he will return. The Arabic phrase Pickthall renders 'it appeared so unto them' (shubbiha lahum) is what all the readings turn on.

For comparison, this is the sharpest divide in the whole unit. It is not a matter of a missing detail, like the ark's size, but of two texts that say opposite things about one event. Christians read the Gospels as eyewitness-based history; Muslims read the Qur'an as God's correction of what earlier communities believed or wrote. Scholars of religion describe both readings and note where each rests. A student's task is to state each accurately: what the passage says, who reads it, and how.

words.d: the Roman execution by nailing or binding to a cross; the Gospels say Jesus died this way
the classical Muslim view that someone else was made to look like Jesus and was crucified instead
the Arabic phrase in 4:157 that Pickthall renders 'it appeared so unto them'
the Christian belief that Jesus rose from the dead on the third day
